sections.h2: What should a McLeod County, MN owner know about property tax before selling?
sections.html:
Two offices decide what you owe: the assessor sets the value and class of your parcel, and the Auditor-Treasurer in Glencoe turns that into a bill and collects it. Real estate tax is paid in two halves, due May 15 and October 15.

Anyone planning a sale in McLeod County should check three things before listing: whether the current half is paid, whether the parcel carries a special assessment, and whether the homestead classification will change after closing. Each one can change what the seller walks away with, and each is easy to confirm with a phone call.

  • Auditor-Treasurer, McLeod County Government Center, 520 Chandler Avenue North, Glencoe: 320-864-1203 for payments, 320-864-1271 for property tax questions.
  • County Assessor: 320-864-1254 for value, classification and homestead applications.
  • Office hours for payments: Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed on holidays.

sections.h2: Where is McLeod County and who lives in its homes?
sections.html:
McLeod County sits west of the Twin Cities in south central Minnesota. It covers 506 square miles, about 491 of them land, and it was created by the territorial legislature on March 1, 1856. Glencoe is the county seat and Hutchinson is the largest city. The other incorporated cities are Biscay, Brownton, Lester Prairie, Plato, Silver Lake, Stewart and Winsted. The South Fork of the Crow River crosses the upper middle of the county, and low rolling hills and small lakes mark the rest of the farmland.

The Census Bureau counted 36,771 residents in 2020 and estimates 36,631 for July 2025. QuickFacts lists 16,162 housing units, a 77.4% owner-occupied rate, and a median owner-occupied home value of $246,100 for 2020 to 2024. Median household income over the same years is $80,084, and 206 building permits were issued in 2025. In 2020, 55.5% of residents lived in urban areas and 44.5% in rural ones, so a seller here might own a lot in Hutchinson, a farmstead near Brownton, or a lake cabin, and each is taxed under a different class.

sections.h2: When is McLeod County property tax due?
sections.html:
Regular real estate and personal property tax is due May 15 and October 15. Farmland follows a later calendar, and manufactured homes use their own dates. McLeod County lists the schedule this way:

McLeod County annual property tax due dates (McLeod County Auditor-Treasurer, Due Dates page)
Property typeFirst halfSecond half
Real estate and personal propertyMay 15October 15
Agricultural propertyMay 15November 15
Manufactured homesAugust 31November 15

Statements go out in March, with a statutory mailing deadline of March 31. Manufactured home statements are scheduled for June, with a July 15 deadline. An owner who has not received a statement still has to pay, so call the Auditor-Treasurer for a duplicate. A seller who is mid-transaction should ask for a copy early, because the buyer's lender and the title company will want to see the parcel number and the amount.

sections.h2: How can I pay McLeod County property tax?
sections.html:
The county lists six ways to pay, and the choice matters when a closing date is close to a due date.

  • In person by check or cash at the Government Center in Glencoe.
  • By mail, made out to McLeod County Auditor-Treasurer. The envelope must be postmarked on or before the due date, and the county warns that postal servicing centers can postmark mail two or three days after drop-off.
  • Online or by phone with a credit card or eCheck. The card fee is 2.5% of the transaction. eChecks cost $1.50 under $10,000 and $10.00 above that.
  • The secure drop box in front of the Government Center. Anything inside at 8:00 a.m. counts as the previous day's business.
  • Direct debit from a bank account, which must be set up at least one month before the due date.
  • Mortgage escrow, where the lender pays from the account it holds.

When searching the parcel online, enter only the number and choose the roll type from the menu, not the letter that follows it.

sections.h2: What happens if a McLeod County tax payment is late?
sections.html:
Penalties apply once a due date passes. Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01, an unpaid half carries a 2% penalty on homestead property or 4% on nonhomestead property, with another 2% or 4% added on the first of the next month. After that, 1% is added each month through December, capped at 8% for homestead and 12% for nonhomestead. The county's penalty page points owners to the state sample tax statement for the current table.

A tax year turns delinquent the following year, and then interest and penalty build monthly while the parcel moves toward judgment and forfeiture. The county will take a payment larger or smaller than the exact installment. A short payment goes first to the penalty accrued for that year. If you mail a payment and it is postmarked within one business day after the due date, state law lets the treasurer abate the penalty once, as long as you have not used that abatement before.

sections.h2: Who sets my value in McLeod County, and how do I appeal it?
sections.html:
The McLeod County Assessor's Office sets market value and class, and the Auditor-Treasurer multiplies that value by the local tax rate. The assessor is Sue Schulz, and appraisers cover assigned areas. Hutchinson and all apartments and commercial parcels go to one deputy assessor, Glencoe, Lester Prairie and Winsted to another, and the township and small city assignments are listed on the county's staff page. State rules require a visual inspection of each property, which the county says usually takes 15 minutes or less. An owner may refuse the interior inspection, in which case the appraiser values from the exterior.

Appeals run in a fixed order under Minnesota Statutes chapters 274 and 278:

  • Local board of appeal and equalization: the town board or city council meets between April 1 and May 31 and must finish within 20 days. It can reduce assessments on petition, but total reductions cannot lower the assessor's aggregate by more than one percent.
  • County board of appeal and equalization: the commissioners and the auditor review what the local board did not resolve. An owner who skipped the local step after being notified may not appear here.
  • Tax Court or district court: the petition and proof of service must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Call the assessor first. Many value questions are fixed with a sales comparison before any meeting is needed.

sections.h2: Which relief programs can lower a McLeod County tax bill?
sections.html:
The largest break for most owners is the homestead classification, which requires that the owner occupy the home by December 1 and file for the following year's taxes. A sale ends it for the seller: under Minnesota Statutes 272.115 the assessor removes homestead status from a property after a transfer unless the new owner applies and qualifies. A buyer who forgets to apply will see a higher bill the next year, which is worth mentioning during negotiation.

McLeod County's FAQ also points to the state property tax refund. An owner who occupied the property as a homestead on January 2 may qualify for a refund based on household income and taxes paid. A separate special refund exists for homeowners whose tax rose more than 12 percent over the prior year. Both are claimed on Form M-1PR, available from the Minnesota Department of Revenue at 651-296-4444. The county does not process refunds.

sections.h2: How do taxes work when a McLeod County house sells?
sections.html:
Minnesota ties the recording of a deed to the tax record. Under 272.12, the county auditor checks for delinquent taxes before transferring the land on the books, and the recorder will not accept the deed without the notation "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered." Deeds that divide a tract also need the treasurer's certification that the current year's tax on the whole parcel is paid (272.121). A sale over $3,000 requires a certificate of value filed with the auditor when the deed is recorded (272.115).

Ask your closing agent how the current year's tax will be prorated, and ask your lender what happens to an escrow balance after payoff. Special assessments for streets and similar improvements appear as a separate line on the statement and follow the benefit to the parcel, so ask the Auditor-Treasurer what remains unpaid on a parcel before you settle on a price.

Truth in Taxation notices go out in November and show proposed taxes for the next year. They leave out special assessments, and a passed referendum can raise the final bill.

faqs.q: Who do I call about McLeod County property tax?
faqs.a: Call the Auditor-Treasurer at 320-864-1203 for payments or 320-864-1271 for property tax questions, and the Assessor at 320-864-1254 for value, classification and homestead. The Government Center is at 520 Chandler Avenue North in Glencoe and is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: What are the McLeod County property tax due dates?
faqs.a: Regular real estate is due May 15 and October 15. Agricultural property is due May 15 and November 15, and manufactured homes are due August 31 and November 15. Statements are mailed in March.

faqs.q: Can I pay McLeod County taxes by credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, online or by phone, with a 2.5% convenience fee on the total. An eCheck costs $1.50 on payments under $10,000 and $10.00 above that. Cash, check, drop box, direct debit and escrow are the other options.

faqs.q: Does a McLeod County sale cancel the homestead classification?
faqs.a: Yes, for the following assessment year, unless the buyer completes a homestead application and qualifies. State law requires the assessor to remove the class after a transfer, and the owner must notify the assessor within 30 days of a sale or change of residence.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to take a McLeod County valuation to court?
faqs.a: The petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Before that, go through the local board in April or May and the county board, because an owner who skips those steps after notice may lose the right to appear.
